'''''Holcus mollis''''', known as '''creeping soft grass''' or '''creeping velvet grass''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the grass family [[Poaceae]]. It is native to [[Europe]] and north [[Africa]].

== Description ==
[[File:Gladde witbol bloeiwijze Holcus mollis.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Young (left) and mature inflorescences]]
''Holcus mollis'' is a [[Rhizome|rhizomatous]] perennial grass found in woods and hedgerows, growing to {{convert|50|cm}} tall. It has rhizomes that occur around {{convert|5|cm|abbr=on|adj=on}} deep in soil or sometimes deeper. Rhizome growth occurs in the period May to November but is fastest from mid-June to mid-July. The rhizomes have many dormant buds that do not develop unless the rhizomes are disturbed and then fresh aerial shoots may arise from the broken fragments. It flowers from June to July.

The main distinguishing characteristics from ''[[Holcus lanatus|H. lanatus]]'' are the presence of rhizomes, and the bearded nodes or 'hairy knees' on the [[Culm (botany)|culm]].<ref name="Hubbard"/>

== Habitat ==
''Holcus mollis'' is favoured by conditions in woodland clearings and at the early stages of [[coppicing]]. Growth and flowering are restricted as the tree canopy develops. It is often a relict of former woodland vegetation, surviving in open [[grassland]] and grassy heaths after woodland clearance despite being a shade lover. It is found mostly on moist, freely-drained acid soils, normally light to medium texture and high in organic matter; it is absent from areas of calcareous or base rich soil, and often grows with [[Pteridium aquilinum|bracken]].

== Insect foodplant ==
The [[caterpillar]]s of some [[Lepidoptera]] use it as a food plant, e.g. the [[Essex skipper]] (''Thymelicus lineola'').

== Status as a weed ==
In a survey of weeds in conventional cereals in central southern [[England]] in 1982, it was found in 1% of [[winter]] [[barley]] but not at all in [[winter wheat]] or [[Spring (season)|spring]] barley.

Each small piece of rhizome is capable of developing into a new plant. Research shows that within {{convert|6|-|8|in}} of the surface, {{convert|1|sqft}} of rhizome infested soil may contain up to {{convert|110|ft|m}} of rhizome, the weight of roots and rhizomes being estimated at 7.5 tons per acre.<ref name="Hubbard">{{cite book |author=C. E. Hubbard |authorlink=Charles Edward Hubbard |year=1976 |title=Grasses |location=Harmondsworth |publisher=[[Penguin Books]] |isbn=978-0-14-013227-4 }}</ref>{{rp|263}}

== Varieties and hybridisation ==
A [[pentaploid]] variant of ''H. mollis'' is common in Britain; it is sterile but [[vegetative reproduction|spreads vegetatively]]. ''H. mollis'' var. ''variegatus'' has striped green and white leaves; it is sometimes cultivated.<ref name="Hubbard"/>

A male sterile hybrid with ''[[Holcus lanatus]]'' exists with 2''n'' = 21 chromosomes.<ref name="Hubbard"/> Hybrids tend to resemble ''H. lanatus'' in their morphology.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.gardenorganic.org.uk/organicweeds/weed_information/weed.php?id=62 |title=Weed Information |access-date=2009-06-23 |archive-date=2012-02-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120223075624/http://www.gardenorganic.org.uk/organicweeds/weed_information/weed.php?id=62 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
